t: #2970 Count the Number of Incremovable Subarrays I
o: A subarray is incremovable if deleting it leaves a strictly increasing sequence (possibly empty). With n ≤ 50, even checking every (i, j) pair by rebuilding the array is at most ~50^3 = 125000 operations — trivially fast. Example 1 is fully sorted, so removing any subarray keeps it strictly increasing: all 10 subarrays count. In example 2, removals must leave a strictly increasing remainder, e.g., removing [8,7] from [8,7,6,6] leaves [6,6], which fails because equal elements are not strictly increasing.
k: With n ≤ 50, an O(n^3) brute force is completely acceptable.
The remainder is the concatenation of a prefix and a suffix, so validity factors into: prefix strictly increasing, suffix strictly increasing, and last prefix element < first suffix element.
Precomputing 'is prefix up to i strictly increasing' and 'is suffix from j strictly increasing' turns each pair check into O(1).

a.i: Try every subarray [i, j], physically remove it, and verify the remaining elements are strictly increasing. Simple and obviously correct.
s: Loop over all start i and end j of the removed subarray.
Build the remaining array by copying elements outside [i, j].
Check it is strictly increasing; count if so.
a.t: O(n^3) — O(n^2) subarrays, each verified in O(n)
a.sp: O(n) for the temporary remainder array

a.n: Approach 2: Prefix/suffix flags + O(1) pair check
a.i: Deleting [i, j] leaves prefix nums[0..i-1] glued to suffix nums[j+1..n-1]. Precompute boolean arrays: pre[i] is true when nums[0..i-1] is strictly increasing, suf[j] when nums[j..n-1] is strictly increasing. Then each pair (i, j) is validated in O(1) by three conditions including the boundary comparison nums[i-1] < nums[j+1].
s: Fill pre[i] for i = 0..n and suf[j] for j = 0..n-1 by single scans.
For each pair (i, j) with i ≤ j, require pre[i], suf[j+1], and (i == 0 or j == n-1 or nums[i-1] < nums[j+1]).
a.t: O(n^2) — precomputation is O(n), then all O(n^2) pairs checked in O(1)
a.sp: O(n) for the two flag arrays

w: Start with brute force to establish correctness, then mention the flag-based method as the natural optimization (it also scales to the Hard version with n up to 1e5 via two pointers/binary search). Pitfalls: treating non-decreasing as strictly increasing (example 3's [6,6]), and forgetting the boundary comparison when both prefix and suffix are non-empty. Follow-up: solve it for n up to 1e5.
